Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents

Haowen Hou    Gen Li    Ruilin Li    Yicheng Liu    Zhen Huang    Shuai Dong    Congcong Wang    Kaiwen Tuo    Hongrui Wu    Zelin Peng    Kanghui Tian    Ji Zhao    Dianyi Wang    Jiaqi Wang Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses while a stronger teacher supplies dense token-level targets [9, 1]. Fully online OPD for interactive agents executes the student in the environment [27], so training covers histories induced by the student’s actions. This alignment becomes expensive over long horizons spanning tens or hundreds of agent turns. A rollout may search a repository, issue web queries, and wait for external tools, so trajectory durations can differ substantially. Synchronous training batches wait for their slowest trajectories, whereas asynchronous pipelines reduce synchronization idle time but still retain the full interaction cost and can introduce stale-policy data [12, 2]. Long and heterogeneous rollouts therefore make training much slower than the model update alone.

Prefix replay offers an off-environment alternative. A separate collection stage records multi-turn trajectories from fixed policy snapshots. During training, the learner selects a stored prefix, generates a response of only one turn from the current student, and evaluates the teacher along that response. The generated response is not executed in the environment. Prefix replay therefore removes variable-length environment rollouts from the learner’s critical path and allows one executed trajectory to support repeated current-student updates.

Prefix replay reduces training cost by constructing updates from stored histories rather than fresh environment rollouts. The quality of these updates depends on two design choices: which histories to collect so that replay reflects situations the student may face while retaining reliable teacher supervision, and which turns to replay so that training focuses on decisions worth learning. Concurrent work ReOPD collects teacher-generated histories and uses a monotone position-decay schedule to favor early prefixes [18]. This design makes both parts of replay static: collection fixes the history source to the teacher, while allocation within each collected trajectory depends only on turn position. These choices are restrictive for long-horizon agents, where early actions can alter many later turns, and consequential decisions can occur at any depth. We address the resulting collection and reuse challenges in turn.

The first challenge is to pair student-relevant histories with confident teacher supervision. Teacher-only trajectories omit states reached after student errors, and this history mismatch compounds over long horizons [22, 14]. To cover situations that the student may face, a frozen student generates an initial segment before the teacher completes the trajectory. These student-induced histories make the replay contexts more relevant to the student, but they may fall outside the teacher’s usual interaction distribution. We therefore pair student-seeded teacher completions with response-level confidence gating: collection broadens coverage toward student-induced histories, while the gate retains responses for which the teacher provides a confident target.

The second challenge is to identify which turns in a long trajectory are worth replaying. Long trajectories interleave routine interactions with consequential diagnoses, corrections, and verification decisions [16]. Replaying every turn spends training computation on steps with limited learning value, while position decay can suppress valuable decisions that occur late in the trajectory [18]. We instead allocate replay after observing the completed trajectory, when later execution feedback and the final outcome can support the value of earlier decisions. After each rollout, we append a selection query to the rollout teacher and reuse its trajectory KV cache to select these evidence-supported turns efficiently.

Together, these components form CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence). CARE-OPD addresses trajectory collection and reuse through reliability-controlled history coverage and hindsight replay allocation. Under matched hardware, CARE-OPD reduces end-to-end training time by 45% and executes 56% as many environment interactions as fully online OPD. On two long-horizon tasks SWE and Deep Research, it improves task success over all prefix replay and fully online OPD methods. We make three contributions:

(1) We analyze the complete prefix replay pipeline as two design problems: collecting student-relevant histories with reliable teacher supervision, and identifying which decisions in a long trajectory are worth replaying.

(2) We develop an adaptive replay method that addresses both problems. Student-seeded teacher completions cover histories induced by student behavior, while response-level confidence gating filters uncertain teacher supervision. Downstream execution evidence then directs replay toward consequential diagnoses, corrections, and verification decisions.

(3) We evaluate the complete training process on Software Engineering and Deep Research tasks. The method improves task performance over fully online OPD and prefix replay methods while reducing wall-clock time and environment interactions. Therefore, we establish prefix replay as a practical environment-decoupled training regime for long-horizon agents.

2 Related Work

2.1 Efficient Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using a teacher’s next-token distribution [9, 1, 7]. Recent extensions adapt OPD to multi-turn agents through teacher intervention, budget-aware rollout and loss allocation, hybrid objectives, and asynchronous rollout pipelines [15, 30, 23, 12, 2]. These methods retain live environment execution during student training.

Prefix replay collects histories independently and trains on current-student responses generated from stored prefixes, keeping environment execution off the training process. Concurrent work ReOPD reuses prefixes from teacher-generated trajectories and assigns each turn a sampling probability that decreases monotonically with its position in the trajectory, thereby favoring earlier turns [18]. We find that this step-decay schedule cannot effectively transfer to long-horizon tasks spanning tens or hundreds of turns. We analyze the complete prefix replay pipeline for long-horizon tasks and identify the limitations in both stages, trajectory collection and reuse. We deal with both: student-seeded teacher completions expand history coverage under response-level confidence control, while downstream execution evidence allocates replay across the completed trajectory.

2.2 Selecting Histories and Updates in OPD

OPD depends on both the teacher target and the histories where the teacher is queried. Fully online OPD uses student-induced histories, while Guided-OPD mixes teacher- and student-generated turns through an intervention curriculum [15]. TrOPD restricts OPD to regions with reliable teacher supervision and uses teacher prefixes for off-policy guidance [26]. These methods control the tension between student-relevant histories and teacher reliability through online intervention and trust regions. CARE-OPD instead constructs a replay pool with student-seeded teacher completions, then reassesses teacher confidence after the current student samples a response.

Several OPD methods also select or weight supervision within a trajectory. TurnOPD allocates rollout and loss budgets using turn-level statistics, SAGE-OPD selects teacher interventions from environment feedback and weights supervision by teacher confidence, and ATOD reweights turns using teacher–student disagreement and uncertainty [30, 28, 23]. Other work masks or reweights OPD supervision using self-uncertainty, token teachability, or position-dependent teacher reliability [13, 25, 19]. These rules derive their decisions from online trajectories, model distributions, or token position. Our replay setting adds an allocation decision over stored prefixes: evidence from the completed trajectory determines where the replay loss is evaluated, and teacher confidence on the newly sampled response determines whether that loss contributes an update.

3 Method

In this section, we first define agentic OPD and prefix replay, then analyze the whole pipeline and identify two limitations of static prefix policies. CARE-OPD addresses them through reliability-controlled history coverage and hindsight replay allocation.

3.1 Agentic OPD with Prefix Replay

OPD in agentic tasks.

We consider tasks x∼p⁡(x)x\sim p(x) in a long-horizon environment. At turn tt, a policy π\pi conditions on history ht=(x,o1,a1,…,ot−1,at−1,ot)h_{t}=(x,o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}) and samples a complete response at∼π(⋅∣ht)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}). The environment returns an observation ot+1o_{t+1}, which may be terminal. A rollout produces trajectory τ=(x,o1,a1,…,oT,aT,oT+1)\tau=(x,o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T},o_{T+1}).

Let NτN_{\tau} be the number of student-generated tokens in τ\tau, and let sks_{k} denote the context before the kk-th token. Let πθ\pi_{\theta} and πT\pi_{T} denote the current student and fixed teacher, respectively. Fully online agent OPD executes the current student to sample τ∼pθ(⋅∣x)\tau\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), then minimizes the token-averaged reverse KL along the trajectory:

ℒOPD(θ)=𝔼x∼p⁡(x),τ∼pθ(⋅∣x)[1Nτ∑k=1NτDKL(πθ(⋅∣sk)∥πT(⋅∣sk))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p(x),\\ \tau\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\frac{1}{N_{\tau}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\tau}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{k})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{k})\right)\right]. (1)

Each learner update therefore depends on a fresh rollout in the environment.

Prefix replay.

Prefix replay removes this coupling between environment interaction and policy update. A separate collection stage generates trajectories from fixed policy snapshots and stores their interaction histories. During training, prefix replay truncates a stored trajectory at turn tt to obtain hth_{t}, then samples a response y∼πθ(⋅∣ht)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}). The teacher is evaluated along yy, but the response is never executed. For a response of length LL, the replay loss is

ℒreplay(θ;ht,y)=1L∑j=1LDKL(πθ(⋅∣ht,y<j)∥πT(⋅∣ht,y<j)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{replay}}(\theta;h_{t},y)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},y_{<j})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid h_{t},y_{<j})\right). (2)

One replay update generates a response instead of a trajectory, and one executed history can support repeated updates as the student changes. Prefix replay therefore removes environment latency from the learner’s critical path. It still leaves open which histories are available and which candidate updates receive training computation.

3.2 Trajectory Collection and Reuse

We first analyze how trajectory collection and reuse determine which replay candidates contribute to student training in prefix replay. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the retained trajectory pool, hth_{t} the prefix of τ\tau before turn tt, and ℬ\mathcal{B} the current replay minibatch. The current student samples y∼πθ(⋅∣ht)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}) from this prefix. We decompose the unnormalized training mass of candidate (τ,t,y)(\tau,t,y) as

q~θ​(τ,t,y,ℬ)=p𝒟​(τ)⏟trajectory samplingqalloc​(t∣τ)⏟turn allocationπθ​(y∣ht)⏟response samplingg⁡(ht,y,ℬ)⏟response acceptance.\widetilde{q}_{\theta}(\tau,t,y;\mathcal{B})=\underbrace{p_{\mathcal{D}}(\tau)}_{\text{trajectory sampling}}\quad\underbrace{q_{\mathrm{alloc}}(t\mid\tau)}_{\text{turn allocation}}\quad\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid h_{t})}_{\text{response sampling}}\quad\underbrace{g(h_{t},y;\mathcal{B})}_{\text{response acceptance}}. (3)

This formulation exposes two limitations of static prefix policies in long-horizon tasks. First, teacher-only collection for 𝒟\mathcal{D} misses student-induced histories. Meanwhile, p𝒟p_{\mathcal{D}} determines the available histories but cannot ensure reliable teacher targets for the responses yy, and broader history coverage can place the teacher in unfamiliar states. History coverage and response acceptance are therefore designed jointly. Second, qallocq_{\mathrm{alloc}} distributes replay across turns of different importance, where a fixed position rule cannot well identify critical turns to learn.

We address the first limitation by expanding teacher rollouts with student roll-ins, and gate the responses with teacher confidence. We address the second with an allocation rule conditioned on the completed trajectory. CARE-OPD uses the whole trajectory and execution evidence to decide where replay occurs. We detail the two components below.

3.3 Reliability-Controlled History Coverage

Prefix replay is on-policy for the sampled response but off-policy for its stored history. A teacher-only pool omits states caused by earlier student actions, and one early deviation can change many later observations. We extend the candidate history distribution with student-seeded teacher completions. A frozen student snapshot generates an initial trajectory segment, after which the teacher continues from the resulting history.

For each trajectory ii, we draw zi∼Bernoulli⁡(α)z_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\alpha), where α\alpha is the student-seeded trajectory fraction. If zi=0z_{i}=0, the teacher generates the full trajectory. If zi=1z_{i}=1, we sample the student roll-in length uniformly as Ki∼Uniform⁡{1,…,Kmax}K_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\ldots,K_{\max}\}. The student acts through turn KiK_{i}, and the teacher completes the trajectory from turn Ki+1K_{i}+1. Let πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} denote the frozen student used for collection. The behavior policy is

πicol(⋅∣ht)={πθ0(⋅∣ht),zi=1​and​t≤Ki,πT(⋅∣ht),otherwise.\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{col}}(\cdot\mid h_{t})=\begin{cases}\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid h_{t}),&z_{i}=1\ \text{and}\ t\leq K_{i},\\ \pi_{T}(\cdot\mid h_{t}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4)

The roll-in rate changes the source of collected histories. Student turns remain as context and never become replay targets, while only turns from the teacher continuation are eligible for allocation. If the student completes the task during the roll-in, we discard the trajectory because it contains no teacher continuation for replay.

Expanded history coverage does not guarantee a reliable update. We observe more low-confidence evaluations on the student responses near the switch points of student-seeded trajectories, as analyzed in Section 4.4. We therefore decide acceptance after sampling the response. For a candidate prefix hh and response y∼πθ(⋅∣h)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h), let pjT=πT(⋅∣h,y<j)p^{T}_{j}=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid h,y_{<j}) at token position jj. Inspired by the turn-level confidence weighting in SAGE-OPD [28], we summarize teacher certainty using the mean top-token probability:

PT​(h,y)=1L​∑j=1Lmaxv∈𝒱⁡pjT​(v),P_{T}(h,y)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p^{T}_{j}(v), (5)

where LL is the response length and 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the token vocabulary. For rejection fraction γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1], let τγ​(ℬ)\tau_{\gamma}(\mathcal{B}) be the γ\gamma-quantile of confidence scores in minibatch ℬ\mathcal{B}. We accept the update when

gγ(h,y;ℬ)=𝕀[PT(h,y)≥τγ(ℬ)].g_{\gamma}(h,y;\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{I}\!\left[P_{T}(h,y)\geq\tau_{\gamma}(\mathcal{B})\right]. (6)

The gate rejects the lowest-confidence fraction γ\gamma and keeps the effective batch size predictable. It treats confidence as a proxy for teacher certainty rather than response correctness. A rejected response contributes no gradient, but its prefix remains available for later replay. Because OPD already computes the teacher logits in Equation 5, the gate adds little inference cost.

3.4 Hindsight Replay Allocation

Reliability-controlled coverage determines where replay can occur, but long trajectories still contain many candidate turns with limited training value. We allocate replay after each trajectory terminates, when later observations and the final outcome are available. A model-based judge receives the task, complete trajectory, execution feedback, outcome, and a fixed selection budget. It selects teacher-generated turns whose diagnosis, correction, or verification is supported by later evidence.

For trajectory ii, let ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i} denote the eligible teacher-generated turn indices. Given selection fraction rr, the judge returns a subset 𝒮i⊆ℰi\mathcal{S}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{i} of size mi=⌈r​|ℰi|⌉m_{i}=\lceil r|\mathcal{E}_{i}|\rceil. This defines

qalloc​(t∣τi)=𝕀[t∈𝒮i]mi.q_{\mathrm{alloc}}(t\mid\tau_{i})=\frac{\mathbb{I}[t\in\mathcal{S}_{i}]}{m_{i}}. (7)

The fixed within-trajectory fraction avoids score calibration across tasks. During training, we first sample a trajectory and then one of its selected turns, preventing long trajectories from receiving extra weight solely because they contain more turns.

We assign each turn a temporary identifier and append one selection query after the rollout terminates. The query reuses the rollout teacher’s trajectory KV cache. We remove the temporary identifiers and selector output before replay, so the student receives the original prefix without future evidence.

3.5 Training Procedure and Cost

Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete CARE-OPD procedure. Environment interactions occur only during pool construction, and hindsight replay allocation runs once per collected trajectory. The selected prefixes can support repeated updates as the student changes. Training therefore retains response-level on-policy generation without placing long environment rollouts on the learner’s critical path.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Data and benchmarks.

We study two long-horizon agentic tasks: Software Engineering (SWE) and Deep Research. For Software Engineering, we partition SWE-Gym [21] into a training set and a validation set of 100 tasks. We collect all training trajectories from the training set and evaluate task success on SWE-bench Verified [11]. For Deep Research, as high-quality data is important, we use a dataset curated from public sources with a quality-control pipeline, detailed in Appendix A. We evaluate answer accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus [3], using Qwen3-Embedding-8B as the retriever and gpt-oss-20b as the judge.

Agent scaffolds.

For SWE, we use OpenHands as the agent scaffold and retain its default system prompt and tools [24]. For Deep Research, we customize the Uni-Agent scaffold [6] and provide three tools: search, open, and find. SFT and OPD training both use a 128K context limit and a 150-turn limit.

Implementation details.

For OPD training, we use 4 GPU nodes, where 1 node is for the teacher, 2 nodes are for student rollouts, and 1 node is for student updates. We optimize for 60 steps. Appendix B lists the complete training configuration. For each training method, we train the policy with 3 seeds and report mean ±\pm sample SD.
